blocks.text: The mechanics of how mortgage loan officers make commission

Your compensation as a loan officer is usually defined in your employment contract. It typically includes a base salary or a draw against future commissions. The primary earnings come from a percentage of the loan amount or a flat fee per funded loan.

Complexity arises from the variables in your plan. If you work in a team, you might have co-origination splits. You might also see branch manager overrides or tiered structures where your percentage increases as your volume grows. Clawbacks for early payoffs also impact your final take-home pay.

The main reason for errors is the reliance on manual data entry. Many brokerages export data from a Loan Origination System into a CSV file. Then, they move that data into Excel. This manual movement creates a high risk of human error.

When you do not have an itemized statement, you cannot verify the math. You see a final number, but you cannot see the individual loan splits that created that number. This lack of transparency leads to distrust and friction between you and your brokerage.
Practical fixes for your commission tracking

items: Create a personal log in Excel or Google Sheets for every loan you originate.
Include the loan ID, funded date, loan amount, and your expected commission percentage.
Compare your personal log against the pay stub you receive each cycle.
Ask your manager for an itemized breakdown if the numbers do not match your log.
Keep a folder in your email titled Commission Statements to maintain a historical record.
